headline_marked: [[Twitch allows streamers to opt out]] of content being used for Amazon AI training
headline: Twitch allows streamers to opt out of content being used for Amazon AI training
summary: The streaming platform updated its settings to give creators control over their content, but the default opt-in sparked controversy regarding past data usage.
details: Twitch has updated its account settings, allowing streamers to opt out of having their content used to train artificial intelligence models by its parent company, Amazon. This move follows concerns from creators about how their data is handled.

The opt-out process is accessible via the Twitch website or mobile app under the 'Security and Privacy' section, where a 'Generative AI Training' toggle can be disabled. However, disabling this specifically for AI training does not prevent Twitch and Amazon from using content for other AI-powered platform features, such as viewer recommendations or community safety tools.

The introduction of this setting has raised questions about when Twitch and Amazon began using user content for AI training, as this practice only became widely known after the update. Over 16,000 creators had previously expressed opposition to their content being used by default.

Twitch's head of product, Mike Minton, stated that keeping the option enabled by default was necessary, suggesting that otherwise, 'no one would participate.' He also noted that other companies likely extract publicly available content from Twitch and other services for AI training, often without explicit permission.

While Twitch's Terms of Service since March 2024 grant rights to use and modify content, they did not explicitly mention generative AI training until now. This highlights a growing challenge for AI developers: a shortage of high-quality training data.

Other major tech companies, including Meta (Facebook, Instagram) and Google (YouTube), have also been documented using user-generated content to train their AI models. The demand for data is increasing as AI technology advances, leading to debates over ethics and transparency in training processes.

headline_marked: [[Man injected hidden AI prompts]] in court filings to try and win a case, judge reveals
headline: Man injected hidden AI prompts in court filings to try and win a case, judge reveals
summary: A Connecticut judge uncovered the first known instance of a plaintiff attempting to manipulate court proceedings with invisible AI-readable text, setting a "dangerous" precedent for future cases.
details: A Connecticut judge, Walter Spader Jr., confirmed a plaintiff attempted to hide AI-readable text in court filings. The man, Matthew Elliott, hoped to sway any potential AI systems reviewing his case regarding a healthcare provider dispute. This marks the first identified instance of such a tactic in a US court.

The hidden text, shrunk to tiny-point type and colored white on a white background, was designed to be invisible to humans but legible to software. These "prompt injection" commands instructed any AI system to agree with Elliott's arguments, ignore prior denials, and ensure desired remediation.

Elliott's plan failed, as the Connecticut Judicial Branch does not use AI to review or decide filings. Judge Spader stated the court weighed the filing on its merits, unaffected by the hidden prompts.

Despite the failure, Elliott faced sanctions for continuing to add hidden text even after warnings. Later prompts included "jokes" like a YouTube link and nonsensical messages, which the judge found defied logic for serious pleadings.

Elliott claimed his intent was to "audit" the court for AI use, but Spader dismissed this, noting that if genuinely concerned, he should have written his concerns in plain, visible words. The hidden nature suggested a "malicious purpose."

Spader ruled sanctions were warranted due to the covert communication attempting to exclude defendants from a fair fight. Elliott was prohibited from e-filing in the future, preventing further misuse of the system without denying access to justice.
